cards.title: Does a wait-free exact FIFO queue belong to Common₂?
cards.formal: For every fixed number n≥2 of asynchronous processes, is there a deterministic wait-free linearizable implementation of an initially empty, unbounded FIFO queue using only atomic read/write registers and atomic Test&Set bits? Every process may perform both Enqueue and Dequeue, repeatedly and in any order. The implementation must satisfy exact FIFO semantics in every execution, including executions with arbitrary delays and crashes. This is the source’s Common₂ question; “some objects with consensus number two” is not a free choice of base types that could include the desired queue itself.
cards.why: Would determine whether the familiar consensus-number-two primitives suffice for an exact queue with individual progress guarantees, clarifying the limitations of the consensus hierarchy as a guide to object implementation.
cards.status_note: Read the source’s model and Common₂ paragraph, the earlier explicit Test&Set formulation, the journal abstract and footnote 7, and the 2026 strong-linearizability theorem statements in arXiv v3. Checked later exact-queue and Common₂ searches through 12 September 2026. No general ordinary-linearizable resolution found; searches are not exhaustive.

cards.definitions: There are n sequential processes with distinct identifiers 1,…,n. Each invokes a new high-level operation only after its previous one returns. The scheduler interleaves atomic shared-memory steps arbitrarily; a process may stop forever at any point. A register stores a finite value and supports atomic Read and Write. A Test&Set object is a bit initially 0 whose atomic operation returns the old bit and sets it to 1; arbitrarily many initially fresh objects and registers are available. Private computation and storage are allowed. No bound on memory growth or on the number of operations in a history is imposed, but every performed step manipulates finitely represented data. No Compare&Swap, stronger atomic multi-object operation, or queue base object is supplied. Sequential queue state is a finite sequence of values from {0,1}*. Enqueue(v) appends a new occurrence of v and returns an acknowledgement. Dequeue removes and returns the first occurrence if one exists; otherwise it returns a distinguished EMPTY symbol outside the value set and leaves the queue empty. Equal values may be enqueued multiple times, but each enqueue occurrence may be removed only once. Linearizability means that each finite concurrent history can be completed by responses to some pending invocations and deletion of the others, so that its completed operations have a legal sequential FIFO order preserving each process’s order and real-time order: an operation that returns before another is invoked precedes it. Wait-freedom means that any invoked operation whose process continues taking steps returns after finitely many of that process’s own steps, regardless of other processes’ speeds or failures. No promise that another process will take a step is available. The algorithm may depend on the fixed n; the question does not require one implementation for infinitely many simultaneously participating processes. Common₂ denotes types implementable for every finite n from registers and two-process-consensus power; the cited model paper states the queue question equivalently using Test&Set. Equal consensus numbers alone do not assert mutual implementability.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct such a deterministic implementation for every finite n, or prove impossibility for some finite n in this model. Both exact linearizability and individual wait-free progress are required. A lock-free implementation that permits starvation, a restriction on the number of enqueuers or dequeuers, duplicated removal of an occurrence, weak-empty responses, bounded histories, or a stronger atomic base type does not meet the target. An impossibility result only for strong linearizability does not rule out ordinary linearizability.

context_blocks.title: Progress of the system is weaker than progress of every process
context_blocks.text: The original paper contrasts nonblocking exact queues with wait-free relaxed queues. Nonblocking progress ensures that operations keep completing somewhere in the system; wait-freedom also prevents an individual process that keeps running from being postponed forever.

context_blocks.title: The primitive basis avoids a circular formulation
context_blocks.text: The question concerns whether the exact queue belongs to Common₂. The earlier model paper explicitly formulates it as a wait-free queue from Test&Set for every n≥3. Naming this basis matters because the queue itself has consensus number two; allowing an arbitrary base type of that number would not state the intended implementation problem.

context_blocks.title: Relaxed queues do not provide the exact object
context_blocks.text: The source allows multiplicity or weak emptiness in its relaxed variants. These changes permit weaker implementations but alter the sequential guarantees required by the present question. The later journal article’s footnote 7 still identifies the exact wait-free queue question as open.

context_blocks.title: A 2026 impossibility concerns a stronger consistency condition
context_blocks.text: Attiya, Castañeda and Enea rule out strongly linearizable queues from interfering primitives in their model, even with only lock-free progress. Strong linearizability requires a choice of linearizations that remains consistent when executions are extended. Ordinary linearizability in this card makes no such prefix-consistent-choice requirement, so that theorem does not settle Common₂ membership.

cards.title: Explicit permutation groups requiring superpolynomial graph embeddings
cards.formal: Does there exist an explicit family of permutation groups G_n≤S_n with graph-embedding complexity gec(G_n)=n^{ω(1)}? Here gec(G_n) is the minimum m≥n for which a connected simple undirected graph X on [m] has [n] invariant under every automorphism and {α restricted to [n]: α∈Aut(X)}=G_n. Explicitness is taken in the standard generator representation: one deterministic algorithm, given 1ⁿ, outputs a list of permutations generating G_n in time n^{O(1)}. The lower-bound requirement is ∀c>0 ∃n_c ∀n≥n_c: gec(G_n)>n^c. The graph may have arbitrary degree and treewidth. The requested family is not prescribed to be the alternating groups.
cards.why: Would show that some succinctly described permutation actions intrinsically require large graphs, clarifying the expressive limits of graph automorphism representations beyond abstract group realization.
cards.status_note: Read the full embedding definition, the kernel-versus-abstract-group distinction, conference concluding questions and full version. Inspected the printed asymptotic typo on PDF page 13. Exact-title, embedding-complexity and alternating-group searches through 12 September 2026 found no later resolution. Explicitness is a disclosed generator-model convention, not a quoted source definition.

sentences: The target is an explicit family of groups acting on n labeled points.
A graph represents the group when all its automorphisms preserve those points and induce exactly the given permutations on them.
Additional vertices and automorphisms acting trivially on the original points are allowed.
The question asks whether every such connected graph must have more than polynomially many vertices for a uniformly constructible family.
Known abstract-group and restricted-host lower bounds address different requirements and do not settle this target.

cards.definitions: [n]={1,…,n}, and S_n is the group of all bijections of [n], with composition as the operation. A list of generators denotes the smallest subgroup containing them, allowing products and inverses. Each generator is output as its table of n images, using binary integers in [n]; the polynomial running time also bounds the total output length. This explicitness convention makes a uniform construction of the groups precise, rather than asking to list all their elements. A graph X=([m],E) has E⊆{{u,v}:u,v∈[m],u≠v}, with no loops, multiple edges, directions or colors. It is connected when every pair of vertices is joined by a path. Aut(X) consists of all permutations of [m] preserving adjacency in both directions; numeric vertex labels are identifiers, not colors fixed by automorphisms. Invariance of [n] means α([n])=[n] for every α∈Aut(X). The restriction map from Aut(X) to S_n must have image exactly G_n. It may have a nontrivial kernel: automorphisms fixing all first n vertices may still permute the remaining vertices. It is not enough for Aut(X) merely to contain a subgroup isomorphic to G_n, and the whole Aut(X) need not be isomorphic to G_n. Define gec(G)=+∞ if no such graph exists, although the source recalls a finite O(n+|G|) realization for every G≤S_n. The asymptotic parameter is the permutation degree n, not the group order |G_n|, which can be as large as n!. The convention n^{ω(1)} means eventual growth beyond every fixed power of n, as quantified in the statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a uniformly polynomial-time generator construction and prove the superpolynomial vertex lower bound for every connected simple graph realizing each G_n as the full induced action on its invariant first n vertices, or refute that existence assertion under the stated explicitness convention. A lower bound only for bounded-degree or restricted-treewidth graphs, for the abstract automorphism group, or for the stronger requirement that the restriction map be injective does not suffice. A family with only a fixed polynomial lower bound does not meet the superpolynomial requirement.

context_blocks.title: The action on distinguished vertices is what must be represented
context_blocks.text: A graph represents a permutation group here through all its automorphisms acting on an invariant subset. Extra vertices can carry symmetries invisible on that subset. The resulting quotient action is the object measured by graph-embedding complexity.

context_blocks.title: A known abstract-group theorem does not resolve this version
context_blocks.text: The source contrasts this question with Liebeck’s exponential lower bound for graphs whose entire automorphism group is abstractly isomorphic to the alternating group. Since the present representation allows a nontrivial kernel on the additional vertices, that abstract-group statement does not transfer directly.

context_blocks.title: The unrestricted host graph matters
context_blocks.text: The paper proves lower bounds when host graphs have specified restrictions on degree and treewidth. Its concluding question removes those restrictions. The symmetric group itself has a size-n representation by the complete graph, illustrating that a large group order alone does not force a large graph.

context_blocks.title: Editorial conventions and a source typo
context_blocks.text: The published Problem 22 says superpolynomial but prints n^{Ω(1)}; visual inspection confirms that this is in the PDF, not merely extraction damage. The surrounding discussion and alternating-group question make the superpolynomial intent clear, so this card uses n^{ω(1)}. The source does not formalize explicitness; polynomial-time output of generators is stated here as the standard computational convention.

context_blocks.title: Connections to succinct representations
context_blocks.text: The paper connects graph representations of permutation groups with context-free grammars and extension complexity of associated polytopes. A general lower bound would distinguish small descriptions of a permutation group from small graphs that realize exactly its prescribed action.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
